Let's parse facts:
[1] AR applications categorized by technology rather than psychological/immersive experience into two broad categories: marker-based and markerless.
[2] Markerless AR apps four subcategories: location-based, superimposition-based, projection-based, outlining-based.
[3] Marker-based use markers placed in environment to trigger augmented experience; device detects marker, desired digital content appears at marker's position in real-world view.
[4] Markers include QR codes, simple color codes, color bars, fiducial markers.
[5] Marker-based easier to build but difficult to maintain because markers prone to damage, damaged marker may make app not work.
[6] Markerless more versatile, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision, allow users to decide where place virtual objects.
[7] Location-based markerless rely on location sensor e.g GPS to detect user's location wrt reference frame, digital content augmented when user at specific location.
[8] Superimposition-based recognize physical objects using CV and superimpose digital content depending on recognized objects.
[9] Projection-based use light projectors to project digital graphics/characters/content onto object/surface/space, e.g holographic projection.
[10] Outlining-based use object recognition to recreate immediate surroundings and digitally enhance view, e.g showing cars around driver not clearly visible low-light.

[1] Non-hand input techniques in VR consist of head tracking, eye tracking, full-body tracking, and sound-based tracking.

[4] Two broad approaches to full-body tracking: motion capture suit (MOCAP) and camera-based tracking.

[6] Camera-based: multiple surrounding cameras observe actor wearing suit with fiducial markers, typically reflective markers, infer overall body movement from markers' movement; examples OptiTrack and Microsoft Kinect.
[7] Sound-based tracking is non-hand input technique in VR that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound for interaction using simple microphones or microphone arrays, which are sets of microphones that capture sound in 360-degree environment.

Lecture VR experience optimisation. Facts:
[1] time-constrained virtual tour optimization approach seeks optimal path that covers max number of POIs while completing within TTH.

[3] virtual tour optimized to cover all vertices of virtual world graph in minimum time may still induce CS if traversal time exceeds threshold above which CS occurs.
[4] no easy way to determine TTH; recommended thresholds may depend on content and movement speed, threshold can be obtained from empirical study ...
[5] planning tour within given TTH, visiting every node/vertex representing POI neither mandatory nor always possible.
[6] importance of node assigned by importance function maps every node, vertex, POI to positive real number, larger higher importance.
[7] importance needed to determine which nodes to cover within given TTH.
[8] total importance of path P containing nodes V1..Vn is sum individual importance f(Vi).
[9] objective identify path takes time <= TTH and has maximum total importance among such paths.
[10] VR path optimization model, each node has two associated quantities: importance and waiting time.
[11] waiting time at node (POI) maximum time user requires inspect/interact object at that node, represented by waiting-time function W maps each node v in V to positive real.
[12] total waiting time W(P) sum individual waiting times.
[13] revised VR path optimization problem maximizes total importance F(P) subject to constraint path's total completion time, T(P)+W(P) <= T_H.
[14] VRPP is generalization of VRP, operations research problem, not all nodes must be visited and route maximizes profit within time constraint, in formulation profit is importance of nodes.
[15] existing VRPP solvers can find optimal path maximizes total importance within TTH.
[16] optimized path must keep user's exposure below TTH beyond which CS may occur and within that time let user visit as many most important POIs as possible.
[17] input optimal-path algorithm for virtual environment is original graph G, fully connected but not necessarily complete, with vertex set V, edge set E, and importance f and waiting time w specified for each node.
[18] desired output optimal path P that maximizes importance value F, covers max number most important POIs, keeps total exposure time (traveling+waiting) less than TTH.
[19] first stage compute complete graph G' by replacing every pair vertices not directly connected with shortest path between those vertices.
[20] algorithm replaces edge weights in complete graph, originally Euclidean distances between node pairs, with travel times t computed using natural walking model, producing final graph G'', edges weighted by travel duration to give realistic experience.
[21] final graph G'', together with importance f and waiting time w of each node, given input to VRPP solver, solver returns optimal path P_opt.
[22] optimal path returned by solver modified by replacing each hypothetical edge between vertices Vi and Vj with shortest path between those vertices in original graph, returns modified optimal path.
